briefs.headline: Oil prices today: Crude falls as US inventories rise; Iran tensions limit losses
briefs.deck: Oil prices declined on Wednesday as US crude stocks increased significantly, adding pressure to the market. Tensions between the United States and Iran, however, continue to limit the drop in prices. Recent hostilities, including drone attacks and interception efforts, have raised concerns about supply disruptions. The Strait of Hormuz remains a crucial route as security risks threaten oil…
briefs.bodyText:
Oil prices declined on Wednesday after industry data showed a sharp increase in US crude and fuel inventories last week, although continued hostilities between the United States and Iran and disruptions to shipping through the Strait of Hormuz limited the fall.
US West Texas Intermediate (WTI) crude futures dropped 56 cents, or 0.65%, to $85.45 a barrel, while Brent crude futures fell 16 cents, or 0.17%, to $92.98 a barrel as of 1.49 am GMT, according to Reuters.
Market sources said US crude stocks increased by 5.28 million barrels in the week ended November 13, citing data from the American Petroleum Institute (API) released on Tuesday.
Gasoline inventories rose by 5.12 million barrels, while distillate stocks increased by 351,000 barrels.
The inventory build put pressure on prices, but concerns over supply disruptions in the Middle East continued to support the market.
US-Iran conflict keeps supply concerns alive
Oil benchmarks had settled higher on Tuesday as the conflict between Washington and Tehran intensified, despite continuing talks involving Iran and mediators Oman and Qatar.
Bahrain's defence force said on Wednesday it had intercepted Iranian aerial attacks on the country, which hosts the US Navy's Fifth Fleet. 
The development followed an exchange of strikes between the US and Iran a day earlier.
Iranian drones attacked a US military radar system in Bahrain on Tuesday, prompting Washington to strike a missile launch site on Iran's Qeshm Island, Reuters reported.
Shipping through the Strait of Hormuz has also faced continued risks. An LPG tanker was hit by a projectile while sailing through the waterway off Oman's coast on Monday, forcing its crew to evacuate.
The strait is a key route for global energy shipments, and attacks on vessels have added to concerns over the movement of oil and other fuel supplies.
“Although regional supply may continue to recover through alternative routes, the latest vessel data suggests that normalization of flows through Hormuz is still not possible under current conditions,” LSEG analysts said in a note on Tuesday.
Houthi drone claims add to regional risks
Supply concerns have also extended beyond the immediate US-Iran confrontation. Yemen's Iran-aligned Houthi group said on Tuesday that it had launched five drones towards two pumping stations along Saudi Arabia's East-West pipeline.
Saudi Arabia has been using the pipeline during the conflict to reroute oil to its Yanbu port for export, bypassing the Strait of Hormuz.
The latest developments have kept attention on the security of alternative export routes as the conflict continues, even as rising US crude and fuel inventories weigh on prices.

briefs.headline: Gold loans drive retail credit, defaults up
briefs.bodyText:
Mumbai: India's retail credit portfolio grew 18.8% year-on-year to Rs 185.2 lakh crore in Sept 2026, led by strong growth in gold loans and consumer durable loans, although early signs of stress emerged in select lending segments, according to a report by CRIF Credit Information Services.
Outstanding gold loans rose 60.6% to Rs 23.3 lakh crore, making them the main driver of retail credit growth. Retail credit expanded 18% during the period, making it the fastest-growing segment for lenders. Consumer durable loans recorded the fastest growth among major consumption-linked categories, rising 44.5% year-on-year and 6.3% sequentially to Rs 1.3 lakh crore.
The report also pointed to emerging signs of stress in select portfolios. Delinquencies in the 91-180-day bucket for personal loans increased to 1.1% in Sept 2026 from 0.8% in June. In gold loans, delinquencies in the 31-90-day bucket rose to 1.3% from 0.9% over the same period.
Secured business loans grew 45.2% to Rs 19.6 lakh crore, while auto loans increased 18.2% to Rs 10.2 lakh crore. Personal loans rose 13.8% to Rs 17.5 lakh crore and housing loans grew 10.4% to Rs 46.4 lakh crore. However, outstanding two-wheeler loans contracted 5.2% sequentially.
Gold loan originations by value increased 27.2% year-on-year to Rs 8.2 lakh crore in Q2 FY27, even as the number of loans originated declined 4.1%. The average ticket size rose 32.7% to Rs 2.2 lakh. Loans of Rs 5 lakh and above accounted for 40.3% of originations by value while representing around 10% of volumes.
Southern states continued to account for more than 70% of the gold loan portfolio. Sequentially, origination volumes remained almost stagnant while their value increased 1.9%. Consumer durable loans also recorded an increase in 91-180-day delinquencies among NBFCs and loans below Rs 50,000. In the two-wheeler segment, early signs of stress remained concentrated in NBFC portfolios and loans below Rs 1 lakh.
Premiumisation was evident across several lending categories, with higher-value loans accounting for a growing share of originations.

briefs.headline: iPhone shipments drop 25%, Samsung regains top spot
briefs.bodyText:
NEW DELHI: 
Apple
's iPhone shipments in India fell 25% in July-Sept. The company shipped about 3.7 million iPhones, down from a record 5 million a year earlier, according to IDC. 
Samsung
 overtook Vivo to reclaim the top spot after 10 quarters, emerging as the only brand among the top 10 to ship more phones than it did a year ago.
IDC attributed Apple's decline to shortages of iPhone 15, 16 and 17, fewer discounts on older models and price increases around the Sept launch. The pricier iPhone 18 Pro and Pro Max together made up more than 30% of Apple's quarterly shipments, with no base iPhone 18 model on sale. Apple moved back to fourth place as several rivals posted steeper declines.
Samsung's shipments rose 7.9%, lifting its market share to 17.7% from 12.6% a year earlier. IDC said Samsung had raised prices more gradually than rivals in the first half of the year and benefited from a wider range of models. Vivo's shipments fell 29.9%, leaving it in second place with a 16.8% share. Oppo held third place as its shipments fell 26.5%.
Overall smartphone shipments fell 23.3% to 36.8 million units, making it India's weakest festive quarter in a decade, according to IDC. Retailers cut back on new orders as higher memory chip costs pushed up phone prices and left brands less room to offer festive discounts. 
Shipments to offline retailers fell 26.7%, compared with an 18.9% decline online. Phones priced below $100 took the biggest hit. Shipments fell 90.9% to 700,000 units, cutting the segment's share to 1.9% from 16.2% a year earlier. The average selling price rose 26.1% to a record $371, while the overall value of the market fell 3.3%.
"Higher ASPs, thin discounts and longer replacement cycles kept demand subdued even through the festive period," said Upasana Joshi, senior research manager at IDC Asia Pacific. IDC expects the decline to deepen in Oct-Dec, with shipments projected to fall more than 25% year on year as stocks of cheaper phones run down. It forecasts full-year shipments of 125-127 million units, down 16-18% from 2025.

briefs.headline: Samsung Heavy Industries eyes India for shipbuilding
briefs.deck: The company's main shipyard in South Korea is fully booked with orders for the next three years.
briefs.bodyText:
New Delhi: Global shipbuilding major Samsung Heavy Industries (SHI) is looking at India to expand its production footprint and cater to growing demand, as its main shipyard in South Korea is fully booked with orders for the next three years. The company is exploring opportunities to manufacture vessels in India, including through a possible investment in the proposed shipbuilding cluster at Kendrapara in 
Odisha
, senior industry executives said. An executive of South Korea's second-largest shipbuilder said its facility had the capacity to manufacture around 60 ships annually.
"India offers new opportunities and we are looking at options here," he added. Last month, during his visit to SHI's shipyard at Geoje, shipping minister Sarbananda Sonowal invited the company to expand its footprint in India by participating in the country's proposed greenfield shipbuilding clusters. There was no official response from SHI to queries from TOI. The South Korean major has begun establishing its presence in India by signing a strategic memorandum of understanding (MoU) with Swan Defence and Heavy Industries (SDHI) to collaborate on commercial shipbuilding and heavy engineering projects.
Responding to queries about the progress of the MoU, SDHI said the ongoing projects with SHI "include, joint submission for Shipping Corporation of India (SCI)'s expression of interest to build eight 88,000 cubic metre very large gas carriers and joint bid for SCI's four dual-fuel ready medium range product tankers.

briefs.headline: Fairfax to sell 13% via 3.4k cr block deal, exit IIFL Finance
briefs.deck: Fairfax Group is divesting its full 13.3% stake in IIFL Finance through a block deal appraised at Rs 3,450 crore. To facilitate this transaction, the Canadian firm has engaged IIFL Capital to handle the sale of over 5.6 crore shares. This divestment follows the company's recent acquisition of close to 61% of IDBI Bank.
briefs.bodyText:
Mumbai: Canada's Fairfax Group, which is in the process of acquiring 
IDBI Bank
, is selling its entire 13.3% stake in IIFL Finance through a block deal worth about Rs 3,450 crore (around $370 million). FIH Mauritius Investments, an arm of Fairfax, has mandated IIFL Capital, a group company, to sell over 5.6 crore shares of IIFL Finance on Wednesday, Nov 18, a term sheet for the deal showed.
While Fairfax is exiting IIFL Finance, it continues to hold 38% in IIFL Capital, currently worth about Rs 4,200 crore, shareholding data on BSE showed.
The block of IIFL Finance shares is being sold at a floor price of Rs 611 per share, a 3.9% discount to the stock's closing price of Rs 636 on BSE on Tuesday.
A little over a month back, Canada-headquartered Fairfax Financial Holdings said that it had entered a deal to acquire a nearly 61% stake in IDBI Bank for Rs 53,000 crore. Since the announcement of the deal, it was expected that the Canadian financial services group would exit some of its holdings in India, mainly to part-finance the IDBI Bank stake acquisition.
On Oct 15, the cabinet committee on economic affairs approved an arm of Fairfax to buy a 30.5% stake held by govt for Rs 26,620 crore and another 30.2% from LIC for Rs 26,440 crore.

briefs.headline: Industry bodies look for tax sops, benefits to boost mananufacturing
briefs.deck: During recent engagements, industry bodies urged the government to introduce strategic incentives aimed at enhancing manufacturing productivity. Proposed measures include tax exemptions, financial assistance, and revising long-term capital gains tax policies.
briefs.bodyText:
New Delhi: Industry bodies on Tuesday sought incentives from govt, including tax, finance and other benefits, to boost manufacturing activity in the country, with some also pitching for rationalisation of long-term capital gains tax on listed shares.
Drawing upon the playbook from the past, CII president R Mukundan sought accelerated depreciation on new plant and machinery, a tool used to boost investment and a limited-period corporation tax benefit for companies creating new jobs. Besides, it wants higher deductions for incremental R&D spend, a demand that is often made but is likely to be rejected after govt set up a new Rs 1 lakh crore fund for the purpose.
During a pre-budget meeting with finance minister Nirmala Sitharaman, Ficci president Anant Goenka also proposed a scheme to attract skilled Indian professionals, who are currently overseas to help strengthen the R&D ecosystem in sectors, such as biotech, AI and semiconductors. "The programme could provide cost-sharing grants for recruitment and relocation, facilitate fixed-term industrial assignments, support technology-intensive entrepreneurship and establish a single-window mechanism for job matching, documentation and relocation assistance."
CII also suggested that the Centre should earmark 3% of GDP towards capital expenditure to sustain the growth momentum. "Alongside enhanced tax deductions for additional women employees, practical support such as worker accommodation, women's hostels and common creche facilities in industrial parks can make a real difference," it said.
In its presentation at the meeting, Ficci sought incentives for 10 "foundation sectors" such as basic chemicals and plastics and synthetic rubber, to reduce import dependence. It has 36 priority products for domestic capacity creation through a "Strategic Manufacturing Capacity Development Programme", which could be either through PLI or phased manufacturing programme.
Further, it proposed a dedicated PLI for advanced chemistry cell components to support battery manufacturing, arguing that Indian manufacturers face a 30-50% cost disadvantage compared with imports from China, besides high capital requirement. It has suggested an outlay of around Rs 12,000 crore.
The suggestions come amid a push for local manufacturing of around 120 products, identified by the department for promotion of industry and internal trade. Discussions are underway among various wings of govt to work out the details.
Ficci has sought the establishment of a new DFI (Development Financial Institution) to support manufacturing. And, weeks after the govt announced the sale of its stake, along with LIC's in IDBI Bank, the erstwhile development financial institution, which had become unsustainable.

briefs.headline: 'Srinivasan, Singh selectively picking facts': Ex-Tata Trusts trustee Khambata
briefs.deck: Former Tata Trusts trustee Darius Khambata rejected allegations that he sought to exploit Venu Srinivasan's brief absence from the Trusts to reshape its structure.
briefs.bodyText:
MUMBAI: "What takes the cake is your suggestion that I strategised to 'temporarily oust' Venu as a trustee to alter the Trusts' constitution." With that line, former Tata Trusts trustee Darius Khambata escalated an already bitter governance battle at the apex of the Tata Group, rejecting allegations that he sought to exploit Venu Srinivasan's brief absence from the Trusts to reshape its structure.
In a sharp rejoinder to vice-chairmen Srinivasan and Vijay Singh, Khambata accused his former colleagues of selectively recounting events and failing to explain the abrupt reversal of their position on a 
Tata Sons
 listing.
Khambata also defended the Trusts' control of Tata Sons, questioned the handling of the succession process involving company chairman N 'Chandra' Chandrasekaran and rejected suggestions that he had acted in concert with Trusts chairman Noel Tata.
'Safeguarding Trusts' stake in Tata Sons rests with trustees'
Former Tata Trusts trustee Darius Khambata said Venu Srinivasan's failure to secure reappointment in Oct 2025 stemmed from former trustee Mehli Mistry's interpretation of an Oct 17, 2024 resolution under which trustees agreed to support one another's reappointment. Mistry's position was based on whether Srinivasan had honoured that commitment and Khambata had "no involvement" in the decision.
Khambata also noted that at the Nov 11, 2025 meeting where he proposed Noel's son Neville Tata as a trustee, Singh had proposed Bhaskar Bhat in what he described as a "mirror image" of his own move. 
If Neville's appointment was evidence of a strategy to take advantage of Srinivasan's absence, he argued, the same charge could apply to Singh's backing of Bhat.
Khambata also cited his own voting record, noting that he supported Srinivasan's reappointment in Oct and Nov 2025 despite having the ability to block it.
He further alleged that Srinivasan, Singh and Noel had themselves failed to abide by the Oct 17, 2024 resolution when they voted against Mistry's reappointment. He said Srinivasan and Singh had not objected to the departures of Pramit Jhaveri and Khambata himself from the Trusts.
Listing remained at the centre of his criticism. Srinivasan and Singh "still give no reason for changing your minds" after backing the anti-listing stance of Tata Sons and Trusts in March 2024, May 2025 and July 2025, only to execute a "volte-face" in April 2026, he said.
Rejecting suggestions that his defence of the Tata model amounted to support for control by Noel, he wrote that "all trustees are equal" and that responsibility for safeguarding Trusts' stake in Tata Sons rested collectively with trustees rather than any individual. He dismissed arguments that such oversight could affect the Trusts' tax-exempt status.
Khambata reopened questions around the succession process involving Chandrasekaran. He maintained there was no contradiction between supporting Chandrasekaran's third term in 2025 and later criticising Tata Sons board's actions in Sept 2026, describing Chandrasekaran's performance as "excellent". His criticism, he said, was directed at the manner in which the board acted in Sept 2026 rather than the chairman himself.
Pushing back against claims that he had remained silent as uncertainty grew over Chandrasekaran's future, Khambata said he wrote to co-trustees on March 2, 2026, seeking discussions after media reports on the Feb 2026 Tata Sons board meeting. "No trustee responded. Was I to hold a meeting by myself?" he wrote.
According to Khambata, trustees later agreed on Aug 13, 2026, to respect Chandrasekaran's decision not to seek another term and begin constituting a selection committee for a successor. He questioned whether Srinivasan, as a Trust nominee director, had drawn Tata Sons' attention to that position before its nominations committee moved to ask Chandrasekaran to continue.
Khambata also rejected suggestions that he lacked independence, saying he had differed with Noel on "several major issues" during 2025 and 2026, while Srinivasan and Singh had themselves agreed with Noel on many of those matters before later breaking ranks. Suggesting that criticism of him stemmed from his decision to "call out" the Sept 17 Tata Sons board meeting, he described the allegations against him as a personal attack.

briefs.headline: BPCL plans to raise ₹9,000 crore through bond sale after nearly four years
briefs.deck: The state-run oil marketer is expected to issue debt with a tenure of around five years to fund its refinery expansion and petrochemical projects
briefs.bodyText:
Bharat Petroleum Corporation (BPCL) is preparing to return to India’s domestic corporate debt market after a gap of nearly four years, with plans to raise around ₹90 billion ($961 million) through a bond sale, according to two merchant bankers familiar with the matter.
The state-run oil marketing company is considering raising the amount in tranches, with the size of the proposed issue still under discussion.
BPCL has begun preliminary discussions with bankers and is considering a bond tenure of around five years. The company is expected to complete the issue before the end of December, one of the bankers said. BPCL did not respond to a Reuters email seeking comment.
The proposed fundraising comes as the company prepares for significant capital expenditure of around ₹250 billion to ₹300 billion annually in the 2027, 2028 and 2029 financial years. The spending will primarily go towards refinery expansion and petrochemical projects, according to a Crisil rating note.
The bonds are rated AAA, reflecting BPCL’s strong position in the domestic oil refining and marketing sector and its strategic importance to the central government.
The proceeds are expected to be used primarily for capital expenditure, with the company’s refinancing requirements remaining limited, a banker said. BPCL currently has no outstanding bonds after its five-year debt security matured at the end of October.
Its last rupee bond issuance was in March 2023, when it raised ₹9.35 billion through three-year bonds at an annual coupon rate of 7.58 per cent.

stories.headline: Sandpapergate: CA opens forum for players to share 2018 ball-tampering accounts
stories.deck: Cricket Australia has announced an independent forum for players involved in the 2018 ball-tampering scandal. This initiative allows players and support staff to share their experiences confidentially. Interim chairman David Boon emphasised the importance of creating a respectful environment for all involved. The forum is designed to address lingering issues without reopening the past…
stories.bodyText:
Cricket Australia (CA) has announced plans to establish an independent forum for players and support staff involved in the controversial 2018 tour of South Africa, offering them an opportunity to share their versions of events in a confidential and respectful environment as the fallout from the ball-tampering scandal resurfaces.
The decision comes in the wake of fresh allegations in Usman Khawaja's autobiography, which have reignited the debate over how much the Australian dressing room knew about the infamous sandpaper incident in Cape Town. CA interim chairman 
David Boon
 said the forum would allow those involved to share their experiences and perspectives, nearly nine years after the scandal rocked Australian cricket.
However, the governing body has made it clear that the initiative will not reopen its original investigation, nor will it lead to fresh sanctions. CA chief executive Todd Greenberg said the forum was intended to give everyone who wished to speak an independent, safe and private platform.
'Time for a circuit breaker': Boon explains CA's decision
Announcing the board's decision in Hobart on Wednesday, ahead of Australia's one-day international against England, Boon said the prolonged controversy had become a distraction for the sport.
"The CA Board agreed to establish a forum that will allow players and staff involved in the events of South Africa in 2018 to share their experiences and their perspectives," Boon told reporters.
"For almost a decade, the fallout from these events has remained part of conversation around Australian cricket ... We believe it is time for a circuit breaker."
In its official statement, CA said the forum would allow those who wished to come forward to share their recollections in a confidential environment. The board has opted against initiating a fresh investigation, believing that a forum would provide a better opportunity for everyone involved to speak constructively and with mutual respect.
Boon stressed that the exercise was not about reopening old wounds but about allowing people to be heard.
"This forum is not about relitigating the past. It is about creating an opportunity for those who wish to be heard to tell their stories in a respectful environment, and for our sport to listen," he said.
The former Australia batter also highlighted the importance of restoring relationships within the cricket fraternity.
"As a former player, I know that one of the most important things cricket gives us is the relationships we build and the mateship that endures long after playing careers end. My hope is that this process can help strengthen those connections and allow us to focus on what lies ahead," Boon added.
Khawaja's claims reopen old wounds
The latest controversy follows claims in Khawaja's autobiography that contradicted the findings of CA's original investigation into the ball-tampering episode during the third Test against South Africa in Cape Town in March 2018.
The initial probe concluded that only then captain 
Steve Smith
, vice-captain 
David Warner
 and opening batter Cameron Bancroft were aware of the plan to use sandpaper to alter the condition of the ball.
Bancroft was caught on television cameras attempting to scuff up the ball with a piece of sandpaper, triggering one of the biggest controversies in Australian cricket history.
Khawaja's account, backed by Warner, suggested that the wider team was at least aware of the attempt to tamper with the ball. However, Test captain Pat Cummins and fellow fast bowler Mitchell Starc have maintained that they knew nothing about the plan.
The revelations have once again brought the contrasting accounts of those involved into focus, prompting CA to provide an avenue for players and support staff who were not interviewed during the original investigation to share their recollections.
'The game is hurting': Greenberg rules out fresh investigation
Greenberg acknowledged that the latest developments had created an uncomfortable situation for Australian cricket, while also accepting that the governing body had a role in shaping the culture that existed at the time.
"Over the past week we have heard several different and conflicting accounts of what transpired in Cape Town in 2018. This has been an incredibly difficult and uncomfortable time for the game and all those involved," he said.
"What happened then and continues to play out now has a lot to do with the culture that existed at that time. A culture that CA played a part in creating."
He also pointed to the Ethics Centre report commissioned after the scandal and the subsequent adoption of 36 of its 42 recommendations as part of the governing body's efforts to address cultural shortcomings.
Greenberg said the new forum was an opportunity to give everyone a voice without turning it into another disciplinary exercise.
"This is a chance to give everyone a voice in an independent, safe and private setting," he said.
"This is not a re-investigation, it is not designed to reprosecute or sanction."
Participation will be entirely voluntary, with no player or support staff member compelled to come forward. CA also does not intend to make the findings or accounts necessarily public.
"Let's be honest - the game is hurting at the moment," Greenberg said.
"It is not good for anyone. We need to find a path through and we need to heal."
The bans that shook Australian cricket
The 2018 ball-tampering scandal resulted in severe penalties for the three players identified by CA's original investigation. Smith and Warner were each handed 12-month bans from elite cricket for bringing the game into disrepute, while Bancroft received a nine-month suspension for his role in carrying the sandpaper onto the field.
The episode also led to widespread scrutiny of Australia's team culture and prompted significant changes within the governing body.
Eight years on, CA hopes the independent forum will help bring closure to a controversy that continues to divide opinions and affect those associated with the game.
"We hope everyone will respect this process and the players will be given the space they need to perform at their best during an important period for the game," Greenberg said.

stories.headline: This is your captain speaking: 'Reluctant leader' Gill is reshaping India's Test culture
stories.deck: Shubman Gill has stepped into the role of captain for the Indian cricket team, showcasing his determination after a tough tour of Australia. He has made a significant mark in Test matches, amassing 754 runs during the tour in England. Gill insists that preparation is key for Test cricket and has publicly supported Rishabh Pant.
stories.bodyText:
When the captaincy was thrust upon 
Shubman Gill
 after a tumultuous Test tour of Australia and before India embarked on the tour of England in 2025 to play five Tests, there were doubts about whether the soft-spoken batter was ready for the burden. Barring leadership exposure in IPL for Gujarat Titans, he did not have much to show on his CV in terms of leadership.
The elegant Punjab batter, though, answered the biggest question in the only way possible: with runs. A staggering 754-run series in England established him as a batter capable of carrying the weight of expectation. Swayed by that, the selectors appointed him as ODI captain too.
Cut to a year later. Gill has now evolved into a leader comfortable taking ownership of decisions, defending teammates publicly and laying down a broader vision for Indian Test cricket.
Ahead of the first Test in Wellington, Gill’s words revealed a captain consumed by the format that matters most to him, much like the man he idolises, Virat Kohli.
ALSO READ: Beware the Basin bluff! Shubman Gill's four-pacer plan looks beyond the first morning
“If someone had asked me a month ago which of the three series I’d most like to win, it would definitely have been the Test series,” Gill said, addressing the media at the Basin Reserve in wet and windy Wellington on Tuesday, two days prior to the start of the two-match Test series vs New Zealand.
“We’re very happy to have won the T20I and ODI series, but there’s nothing like winning the Test series as well,” the skipper stressed.
The remark was telling. In ODIs, Gill, despite being the No. 1 batter in the format and the captain, still operates in the shadows of Virat Kohli and 
Rohit Sharma
, two giants who continue to define the format and drive the narrative. In T20Is, despite once being viewed as a future leadership option and serving as Suryakumar Yadav’s deputy, team balance and combinations pushed him out of the squad all together ahead of the T20 World Cup.
But Test cricket has become Gill’s domain.
It is in the longest format that he has made the most consequential decisions as captain. Over the last year, Gill has repeatedly stressed the importance of adequate preparation before Test assignments.
“Whenever we get the opportunity, I’d like our preparation to be as thorough as possible,” Gill said. “It’s not easy coming into a different time zone, adjusting your body clock, adapting to the conditions and dealing with the physical and mental stress that comes with it. An extra three or four days definitely helps.”
The same conviction was evident in the way he backed 
Rishabh Pant
. Despite Pant’s occasionally uneasy equation with coach Gautam Gambhir and his removal as vice-captain, Gill emphatically endorsed the value that the mercurial wicketkeeper-batter brings to the team in SENA countries. “He’s probably one of the most experienced and senior contenders in the team,” Gill said, adding that Pant has played over 50 Tests. “Given the quality he brings, he’s scored hundreds all over the world. He’s got hundreds in Australia, South Africa and England. This is probably the only country where he hasn’t.”
Gill has tied his leadership goals to India’s World Test Championship ambitions. He has been part of the 2025 Champions Trophy and 2023 and 2025 Asia Cup wins and Border-Gavaskar Trophy triumphs in 2021 and 2023. But he has also played in two WTC finals that India lost in 2021 and 2023, where he could not contribute much as an opener.
It remains unfinished business for him.
“I believe if we win these two Test matches, we have a very good chance of making the World Test Championship final,” he said. “That’s why we pulled most of the players out of the ODI side early so they could have the best preparation possible.”
If India can secure a place in the WTC final and ultimately lift the mace, Gill’s impact will be measured beyond just his numbers with the bat.

stories.headline: India brace for toughest ‘Test’ in Hadlee land
stories.deck: Their last Test win here came in early 2009, under Dhoni in Hamilton, a result that was enough to also give them their first series win in New Zealand in more than four decades. India haven’t won any of the six subsequent Tests and have lost the last four on the trot, so if Gill’s men have to buck that depressing trend, they need to find higher gears
stories.bodyText:
Test cricket in New Zealand translates to green, seaming decks. To pitches with not just grass, but a fair amount of bounce. To faster bowlers holding sway, to batters being put through a severe examination of technique and character, of skills and temperament. The names roll off the tongue easily. Lance Cairns and Ewen Chatfield and Martin Snedden, then from later generations Chris Cairns and Simon Doull and Chris Martin and Danny Morrison, Shane Bond and Tim Southee and Trent Boult and Neil Wagner. Matt Henry and Kyle Jamieson. Occasionally, quality spinners such as Daniel Vettori and John Bracewell.
And the big daddy of them all, Sir Richard Hadlee.
Just as Martin Crowe was to New Zealand batting – and remains so, despite the emergence of Stephen Fleming, Ross Taylor and Kane Williamson as worthy successors – New Zealand’s bowling has perennially been about Hadlee and the rest. The master of swing, of course, but also with the rare ability to get the ball to jump and bite off the seam. Grateful for help from the conditions, but not necessarily reliant on it. One of the great all-rounders of his generation, alongside Ian Botham and Imran Khan and Kapil Dev, a legend of Nottinghamshire and New Zealand and world cricket. The champion without parallel.

briefs.headline: Dhoni: Like Rajini, Chennai’s adopted son gave the fans as much love as he received
briefs.deck: MS Dhoni has been a pivotal figure for the Chennai Super Kings since the IPL began in 2007. Revered by fans, he guided the team to several championships, especially after his impactful return in 2018, which spurred a revival. Even facing recent obstacles, Dhoni's role is crucial in shaping the team moving forward, illustrating the shifting trends in T20 cricket and the hurdles that lie ahead.
briefs.bodyText:
Chennai always loved its cricket, just that it never had its Super King. Till 
MS Dhoni
 happened.
In 2007, as the 
IPL
 was conceptualized, franchises across the country were busy getting their ‘icon players’ into their squads. Mumbai had Sachin Tendulkar, Kolkata had Sourav Ganguly while Bengaluru boasted of Rahul Dravid. But Chennai didn’t have one. And that’s when N Srinivasan, mainstay of India Cements — the then owners of 
Chennai Super Kings
 — decided to bring in Dhoni from the auction.
It wasn’t without a contest. KKR went hard for the Jharkhand cricketer — but they simply didn’t have the purse that CSK had reserved for Dhoni. “He had just won the T20 World Cup, it was a no-brainer that we would go for him. Of course, we never thought he would become the success that became, but his commitment always attracted us,” Srinivasan once told TOI.
Chennai has had its share of cricket stars in former India captains Srinivas Venkataraghavan and Krishnamachari Srikkanth. But what it lacked was the runaway success that makes a sportsman the king of the hearts. “That’s exactly where Dhoni comes in,” Srikkanth, part of early-day CSK management, told TOI. 
“The people of Chennai started to identify success in cricket with Dhoni as CSK went on its trophy winning run. That’s how the aura of Dhoni happened.”
The Dhoni-Chennai love affair was almost instant. In 2008, the IPL, a revolutionary sporting idea that immediately exploded into the imagination of a nation at large, found a welcoming home in Chennai, the mostly sedate southern city.
For Dhoni, it was a quiet stardom that was previously reserved for film stars and filmstars-turned-politicians. Pictures of him riding his bike into the hotel for a CSK press conference would hog the newly-begun entertainment supplements of newspapers. The timing of it all seemed almost manipulated. Suddenly, Chennai had a sporting hero of their own, India’s captain.
In the league’s inaugural season, an improbable run to the final followed. The following season, a last-four berth and the first title in 2010. The Jharkhand bomber had completely taken over Chennai the way a Marathi bus conductor from Karnataka — Rajinikanth — conquered Chennai hearts way back in the 1980s.
“In many ways, Dhoni’s superstardom can be equated with Rajini’s. It shows the openness of Chennai’s people. They are always ready to appreciate talent,” Srikkanth said.
The success got sweeter through the early 2010s as CSK again became champion in 2011 and was almost a permanent fixture in the final. Dhoni was at the centre of it all.
That is, until the 2013 spotfixing scandal led to CSK’s dismissal after the 2015 edition. The obits were written and everybody was convinced that it would never be the same again for the Chennai franchise. Dhoni may have turned out for Pune Supergiants for those two years of the ban, but always maintained: “Chennai will always be my first home.”
Paradoxically, it was in these two years of ‘exile’ that the cult of Dhoni grew in the hearts of the CSK fans. In fact, by 2018 when Dhoni was back in the CSK yellow, it seemed that IPL itself was waiting for it. Dhoni, in his No. 7 jersey, became the image of brand IPL’s growth and its ability to stave off its detractors.
Dhoni’s arc from 2018 onwards to help CSK win back its glory days stumped everybody, barring Srinivasan. He assembled a ‘dad’s army’ and when many found the 30-plus picks like Shane Watson, Imran Tahir, Harbhajan Singh, Ambati Rayudu, Faf du Plessis as defying sporting logic, Srinivasan held firm. “We know what Dhoni is doing and we believe in it. A combination of experience and ability is gold dust, just see what happens,” he said.
What followed were three titles in six years — CSK’s golden era and Dhoni’s high noon. His manoeuvrings on the field, the ability to conjure lastover sixes and bowling changes made it a five-all in the title count with Mumbai Indians. But on the sidelines, there was a revolution brewing in T20 cricket. Despite his tactical brilliance, he probably missed a trick as the game moved on from methodical madness to monstrous power.
‘Brand CSK’ has struck its lowest ebb over the last three years — three back-to-back failures to make the last-four is unthinkable by their own lofty standards. Injuries have taken a toll on the maestro’s body and despite his initial assurance that he would play this season, the 45-year-old has opted out.
But make no mistake, he is leading CSK’s revival. Everything is being overseen by Dhoni. The competition is now more demanding, tougher.
Dhoni, the mastermind, will be there in the dugout mentoring his new bunch.

briefs.headline: Will Siraj play first Test vs NZ? leaves final call to Shubman Gill
briefs.deck: Morne Morkel addressed concerns regarding Mohammed Siraj's form ahead of the first Test against New Zealand. He emphasized that the final decision on lineup rests with captain Shubman Gill. Morkel expressed confidence in the team's bowling resources to secure the necessary wickets for victory. He also mentioned the importance of managing external distractions to maintain focus. Adjustments to…
briefs.bodyText:
India bowling coach 
Morne Morkel
 did not give a clear answer on 
Mohammed Siraj
's place in the playing XI for the first Test against New Zealand, saying the final decision rests with captain 
Shubman Gill
.
With questions being raised about Siraj's recent form, Morkel was asked whether the fast bowler's place in the team was under scrutiny. However, the bowling coach backed Siraj's abilities and left the selection call to the captain.
"Siraj is a world-class performer, whenever he has stepped in India jersey, whenever he has played," Morkel said on the eve of the first Test.
He also made it clear that he was confident about India's bowling resources and believed the attack had enough firepower to take 20 wickets.
"My feedback to Gautam (head coach Gautam Gambhir) was that we have enough in attack to take 20 wickets. Ultimately the call will be taken by Shubman," he said.
'Don't overthink conditions'
Morkel also warned the bowlers against thinking too much about the conditions. He wants them to trust their plans and focus on executing them rather than getting distracted by the pitch or the weather.
"Don't overthink conditions," Morkel said.
He believes getting off to a strong start will be important, but also pointed out that a Test match can change at any stage. 
India will need bowlers who can make an impact not just in the opening sessions but also towards the end of the game.
"The best way of winning is to set the tone in the first session, but the first session doesn't always win a Test. You need guys who can produce a magical spell on the fourth or fifth day," he added.
'We cannot afford to lose points': Morkel
Morkel urged the Indian bowlers to ignore external distractions and concentrate on their plans. With India competing for a place in next year's World Test Championship final, he stressed that the team cannot afford to drop points.
India are currently fourth in the World Test Championship standings and will be looking to make the most of the two-Test series against New Zealand.
"We need to block outside noise and get the ball in the right areas. We cannot afford to lose points. The team needs to take ownership and get quicker to the mark. The responsibility lies with the bowler and the captain," he said.
Morkel also spoke about the challenges of bowling in Wellington, where strong winds can affect the fast bowlers. He explained that bowling against the wind can help generate movement, but bowlers need to make adjustments to their approach.
"When you bowl into the wind, you get a bit of shape. Your thought process is important. You can hold your actions a bit longer," he said.
He added that the wind was not as strong as it had been in recent weeks. The Indian bowlers, therefore, would need to keep assessing the conditions and adjust their lengths during the match.

briefs.headline: Controversy! Magnus Carlsen forfeits Fast Classic game against Bibisara
briefs.deck: Magnus Carlsen forfeited his Fast Classic game against Bibisara Assaubayeva after achieving a decisive lead. He expressed that the decision was due to the game's irrelevance after the day's results were secured. Carlsen's forfeit followed a disappointing performance in the group stage that affected his classical rating significantly. The Fast Classic format features shorter time controls…
briefs.bodyText:
NEW DELHI: 
Magnus Carlsen
 was involved in another controversy at the Total Chess World Championship Tour Pilot in Budapest after forfeiting his Fast Classic game against Kazakhstan's Bibisara Assaubayeva on Tuesday.
The Norwegian grandmaster decided not to play the game after securing the day's result through blitz and rapid games. The unplayed Fast Classic game had no impact on his classical rating, as forfeited games are not included in rating calculations.
Carlsen won the first three blitz games and drew the fourth before winning both rapid games. This gave him an 11.5-0.5 lead. With only eight points available in the Fast Classic game, Assaubayeva could no longer win the day's contest.
Assaubayeva was awarded the victory by forfeit, leaving Carlsen with an 11.5-8.5 win for the day.
Carlsen, who was scheduled to play with White, explained his decision to Norwegian broadcaster TV2. He said there was no point playing a game that could no longer change the result.
“There will be no classical game as I understood, the match is over. The only consequence of not showing up is that you will lose a totally useless game. 
I think that if you play a World Championship and it counts for points and such, I can understand,” Carlsen said.
“In the end, if you play games after, it shall not be rated because it’s always been like that. And if they want to do things differently here. This is my decision on this topic.”
Why did Carlsen forfeit the game?
Carlsen's decision came after a difficult run in the Fast Classic format at the Budapest event. The 35-year-old had struggled during the five-day group stage, where he failed to win any of his 10 games. He drew nine games and lost one against Armenia's Haik Martirosyan.
The results cost him 21.8 Elo points, taking his live classical rating to 2801.2. He finished fifth in Group C and came close to dropping below the 2800 rating mark.
American grandmaster Fabiano Caruana also came close to overtaking Carlsen as the World No. 1 in the classical ratings during the group stage.
The decision to forfeit the game against Assaubayeva also meant Carlsen avoided another possible rating loss. A draw would have cost him 3.5 rating points, while an over-the-board defeat would have cost him 8.5 points.
However, Carlsen said his decision was based on his objection to playing a game that would not count towards the classical rating after the day's result had already been decided.
Under FIDE's rating regulations, unplayed games, including forfeits, are not included in rating calculations. As a result, Assaubayeva received the tournament points for the game, but neither player's classical rating was affected.
What is Fast Classic chess?
Fast Classic is an accelerated form of classical chess. Players start with 45 minutes on their clock and receive a 30-second increment after every move.
The format was part of the Total Chess World Championship Tour Pilot in Budapest. Unlike regular classical chess, the shorter time control makes the games faster while still requiring players to manage their time and make decisions under pressure.

briefs.headline: The last whistle for Thala: Dhoni's Chennai story was always bigger than cricket
briefs.deck: The No. 7 jersey will no longer be worn, but the whistles, the yellow flags and the memories of those evenings when Dhoni walked out to bat with a game hanging in the balance will endure. CSK may be moving into a new chapter, but the man who shaped its identity will forever remain.
briefs.bodyText:
NEW DELHI: On Babu Jagjeevan Ram Street, a short distance from Chepauk, Mohammad Arif has a shop named 
Dhoni
 Sports. He set it up nearly a decade ago, driven by his admiration for the former India captain. There was one hope behind the name, too: that Dhoni would someday walk through its doors.
At Dakshin, the South Indian restaurant at Chennai's Crown Plaza, MD Suresh had a different way of being connected to the cricketer. For years, he prepared the filter coffee Dhoni liked. 
Chennai Super Kings
 stayed at the hotel for nearly a decade during their home assignments, and Dhoni enjoyed watching Suresh make the brew.
Nabeel VP, originally from Malappuram and now settled in Chennai, found his own place in the city's Dhoni and CSK fan culture. A member of the All Kerala Dhoni Fans Association and connected with the Whistle Podu Army, he was part of groups that organised charity initiatives around Dhoni's birthday.
In 2020, he travelled from Shimla to Delhi after learning Dhoni was flying out of the capital, hoping to meet his hero. He waited at the boarding gates with files documenting their work. Dhoni stopped, heard him out, patted his shoulder and said, “Keep up the good work”. 
He even wanted to keep the file as a memory. For Nabeel, that brief meeting became a moment to cherish.
Therein lay something of the Dhoni phenomenon. In Chennai, it was the familiarity of a favourite coffee, the hope of a visit to a neighbourhood shop, the yellow jersey and the whistles that followed him. It was also a fan culture that reached beyond the city, bringing people together through their admiration for one cricketer and one team.
Friendly Airport Portrait with Award
For Nabeel, the appeal of Dhoni and CSK was also about the experience of being in the stands. “Movies are for two hours, right? But this happens right in front of us for four hours; four hours of entertainment.”
It began, though, with a decision at the inaugural IPL auction in 2008. Chennai Super Kings secured Dhoni for $1.5 million, around Rs 6 crore, making him the most expensive player at the auction. On November 17, 2026, the franchise confirmed that Dhoni had retired as a player and would take up a mentoring role from 
IPL
 2027. His last appearance had come in CSK's final fixture of IPL 2025; he did not play in the 2026 season.
Five titles, and the nights that made them
The first glimpse of what Dhoni could mean to Chennai came before CSK had won anything. In 2010, with a place in the playoffs at stake against Kings XI Punjab, he made an unbeaten 54 to take his side home. It was the sort of innings that would become familiar over the next decade and a half: a difficult situation, a finish that seemed to arrive almost on cue, and a captain who rarely gave away what he was thinking.
By the end of that season, CSK had their first IPL title. Dhoni's contribution was not always about the runs he scored. In the 2011 final against Royal Challengers Bengaluru, he promoted himself to No. 3 and made 22 off 13 balls as CSK posted 205 before winning by 58 runs. The title defence made them the first team to win consecutive IPL crowns.
Dhoni Sports Storefront
Then came the two-year suspension, and the sight of Dhoni in a different yellow-less jersey. His return in 2018 was one of the defining chapters of the CSK story. The team was labelled a 'Dad's Army', but Dhoni and his group answered on the field. Against Royal Challengers Bengaluru that season, chasing 206, CSK were 74/4 when he joined Ambati Rayudu. Their 101-run partnership turned the chase around. Dhoni finished unbeaten on 70 off 34 balls, hitting the winning six with two deliveries to spare.
There was another reminder of his ability to make a game feel unfinished until the very last ball in Bengaluru the following year. Chasing 162 against RCB, CSK had slipped to 28/4. Dhoni made 84 not out off 48 balls, taking the chase to the final over. With 26 needed, he struck 24 off the first five deliveries - four, six, six, two, six - before CSK fell one run short. It was a defeat, but one that captured the hold he had over a game, and over the people watching him.
The late-innings numbers put that reputation into perspective. Dhoni scored 3,468 runs in overs 16 to 20, more than any batter in IPL history between 2008 and 2025. Those runs came at a strike rate of 175, with 208 sixes. In the 20th over alone, he scored 844 runs at a strike rate of 243.2. The next batter on that list, Ravindra Jadeja, has 407.
MS Dhoni Leads Death-Over Scoring
Even as his batting role changed in the later seasons, the capacity for one last intervention remained. In the 2021 Qualifier 1 against Delhi Capitals, CSK lost their way after being 113/1, slipping to 160/6 in the 20th over. Dhoni walked in ahead of Jadeja and made an unbeaten 18 off six balls, hitting three fours and a six to take CSK into the final. It was a small innings by his standards, but a familiar finish.
That ability to take a game deep was only one part of his contribution.
Behind the stumps, Dhoni's sharp hands and anticipation became as much a part of the CSK identity as his batting. In the 2018 final against Sunrisers Hyderabad, he stumped Kane Williamson for 47. It was a significant moment in the match, and another marker in Dhoni's growing record: he has 47 IPL stumpings, the most by any wicketkeeper in the league. His 201 designated-keeper dismissals are also an IPL record.
The captaincy record grew alongside those performances. Dhoni led CSK in 235 IPL matches, winning 136, and took the franchise to 10 finals as captain. Five of those ended with the trophy in his hands - 2010, 2011, 2018, 2021 and 2023. He also led CSK to Champions League T20 titles in 2010 and 2014.
The numbers place him at the top of several IPL leaderboards. But for CSK, the story was also about the continuity: the same captain returning after a suspension, rebuilding after difficult seasons, trusting players in pressure situations and taking the team back to the final stages year after year. Across 18 IPL seasons, he scored 4,865 runs in 248 matches for the franchise. The association outlasted changing teams, changing roles and changing generations of supporters.
Tea Service
A captain measured beyond seasons and trophies
And then there are the people who made the journey their own. Nabeel had said in 2023 that he knew Dhoni was entering the last phase of his playing career. “It's his last phase. I don't know if this is his last season or not, but it's the last phase. 
So we have to make this season more memorable.”
That season has now passed, and the playing chapter is over. Dhoni will remain with CSK in a mentoring role, but the sight of him walking out in the yellow jersey, with a game hanging in the balance, belongs to the past.
The No. 7 jersey will no longer be worn, but the whistles, the yellow flags and the memories of those evenings when Dhoni walked out to bat with a game hanging in the balance will endure. CSK may be moving into a new chapter, but the man who shaped its identity will forever remain.

briefs.headline: My aim is to just stay focused, says shooter Vivaan Kapoor
briefs.deck: He credits training camps under Olympic champion Cernogoraz for his quota-winning performance at Worlds
briefs.bodyText:
Focus, precision and razor-sharp reflexes are the bedrock of shooting. India’s Vivaan Kapoor, however, believes the game is as much about one’s mindset.
The Jaipur-born shooter calls himself a “glass-half-full guy”, and he had every reason to live up to that description after his silver-medal finish in the men’s trap event at the recent ISSF World championships.
Vivaan came within touching distance of gold before losing to Kuwait’s Abdulrahman Alfaihan in a shoot-off.
The silver, however, was no small feat. He secured a quota place for India at the 2028 Los Angeles Olympics and became only the fourth Indian man to win a trap medal at the World championships.
While the quota ensures India’s representation in the men’s trap event at Los Angeles, it does not guarantee Vivaan a place in the team. He will have to come through the National trials to earn the right to represent the country.
“Standing on the podium was a dream, and there is not an iota of disappointment at missing out on gold. When you miss a target, you control your emotions and reset for the next shot.
“Just like that, now, to make the Olympics cut, there’s no pressure as such.
“I will not change my approach but there are some technical aspects that I need to work on. My aim is to just stay focused,” Vivaan told The Hindu.
Having changed coaches just six months before the championships, Vivaan underwent an intense build-up, with three training camps under Olympic champion Giovanni Cernogoraz, two in Croatia and one in Italy.
“Shooting alongside him in camps helped me get used to competing against top shooters. It made me calmer and better at controlling myself. Peter Wilson, our National coach, also helped me a lot with the mental aspect,” Vivaan said.

briefs.headline: Top Indian paddlers write to adhoc panel suggesting a slew of changes
briefs.bodyText:
The omission of Indian paddler Manika Batra from the Indian table tennis team and named as a reserve player for the Aichi-Nagoya Asian Games, among other things, triggered a major controversy and was followed by the suspension of the Table Tennis Federation of India (TTFI) by the Sports Ministry.
Ranked just outside the world top 50 (51st) at the time of selection, the Indian star was dropped, inviting widespread criticism of the TTFI’s selection policy. This is the second time in four years that the TTFI has been suspended and an ad-hoc committee appointed to run the sport.
To ensure that such controversies do not recur, some of India’s leading players (men & women) have proposed a series of changes to the existing selection framework (a copy of which is with The Hindu), placing their recommendations before the erstwhile TTFI and now the ad-hoc committee recently.
They firmly believe the proposed changes will bring greater transparency to the selection process and minimise the scope for potential conflicts.
One of their significant recommendations is to introduce clearly defined world-ranking brackets, with 40 points for players ranked 1-50, 36 for those placed 51-60 and 32 for 61-70, reducing progressively to four points for the players ranked between 131 and 150.
They believe this will reward international performance more precisely and encourage players to improve their rankings.
The proposal, however, retains the TTFI’s existing domestic ranking points system, with 50 points for the national No. 1, 45 for No. 2 and progressively reducing to five points for the 10th-ranked player.
It also recommends continuing with the TTFI’s best four results from seven domestic tournaments.
The proposed selection framework gives 50% weightage to domestic rankings, 40% to world rankings and the remaining 10% to the Selection Committee.
The biggest thrust, however, is on doubles.
The top players want any pair ranked in the world’s top five to be directly considered for selection, depending on the tournament.
For the World and Asian Championships, they have proposed direct selection for top-eight pairs wherever separate doubles entries are permitted.
Published - November 18, 2026 12:20 am IST
